When I'm turning an engineering change list into release notes, how do I decide what's user-facing and what's internal? I keep either dumping everything in or cutting things users actually needed to know.

Use one test per item: **does a user see it, feel it, or have to do something about it?** If any of the three is yes, it's user-facing. If none is, it's internal, however much engineering effort it took.

Applied to the usual categories:

- **New features and behaviour changes** — user-facing by definition. If a button moved, a default changed, or a limit changed (uploads up to 25 MB instead of 10 MB), users will notice; the notes should notice first.
- **Bug fixes** — user-facing if a user could have hit the bug. 'Fixed a crash when deleting a shared notebook' matters to anyone who shares notebooks. 'Fixed a race in the job scheduler that never surfaced' does not.
- **Performance work** — user-facing only when the improvement is perceptible and specific ('search is faster on slow connections'). 'Upgraded the database driver' is the same project described from the inside; it fails all three tests.
- **Refactors, migrations, dependency upgrades, code removals** — internal, unless they change a requirement or drop support for something. The moment a refactor ends support for an old printer, an old OS, or an old file format, it stops being internal: someone out there is using that thing.

Two failure modes to guard against. The first is effort bias: the item the team spent six weeks on (a storage migration) feels important, but importance to the team is not visibility to the user. The second is the reverse — a one-line change that retires an API token or renames a template variable is trivial to build and critical to publish, because it forces user action. Those go at the top of the notes, not in proportion to their size.

A practical discipline: classify every item on the list, publish the user-facing ones, and keep a named excluded list with a one-line reason per item. Then 'we left it out' is a decision you can defend, and anyone reviewing the notes can check the whole list was accounted for instead of wondering what fell off the truck.

One item on our change list just says 'miscellaneous fixes'. My manager wants it in the release notes as-is. What should I actually do with an item like that?

Don't publish it, and don't quietly drop it either — send it back to its source. 'Miscellaneous fixes' in release notes tells users nothing, and it usually hides one of two things: a bundle of small fixes nobody itemised, or a fix someone was embarrassed to describe. Both are worth unpacking before they reach users.

Concretely:

1. **Ask the author for the itemised list.** The fixes exist somewhere — a pull request, a ticket, a commit message. 'Misc fixes' is a summary written for the change list, and the detail is almost always recoverable in a few minutes.
2. **Classify what comes back like any other item.** Most bundles turn out to be two or three real fixes (user-facing, publish them properly) plus internal tidy-up (excluded, with the reason recorded).
3. **If the detail genuinely can't be recovered before the deadline**, publish the release without the item but record it in your excluded list as 'unitemised — detail requested', not as a clean internal exclusion. That keeps your coverage honest: the item was accounted for as unknown, not laundered into a category it might not belong to.

Why not just print 'miscellaneous fixes'? Because it trains users to ignore your notes. Every content-free line lowers the chance they'll read the line that matters — the one that says their export format is gone or their token stops working. Release notes are a trust instrument: specific when you know, silent when you don't, and never padded.

And if your manager insists: offer the honest version of the same sentence. 'Several small fixes' is still weak, but pairing it with the count once you have it — 'three small fixes to invoice rounding, reminder timing, and client import' — usually turns out to be all the item ever contained. The fix is nearly always available; it just isn't in the change list yet.

Why do you keep telling me to lead release notes with the breaking changes? Marketing wants the shiny new features first and the warnings at the bottom where they 'don't scare people'.

Because the order of release notes is a triage decision, not a marketing one. Readers skim from the top and stop early — the people most at risk from a breaking change are the ones least likely to reach a warning at the bottom.

Think about what each section demands of the reader:

- **Breaking changes demand action before updating.** Reissue a token, export in the old format, re-pair a device, stay on the old version until a plugin catches up. If a user updates first and reads later, the warning is worthless — the export format is already gone. Action items go where they'll be seen in time to act: first.
- **New features demand nothing.** They are discovered happily whenever the reader gets to them, and they lose nothing by sitting below a two-line warning.

Marketing's fear is real but misaimed. A warning at the top doesn't scare people off the release; it signals that you respect the ones with something to lose. What actually scares users is the other experience: updating on a Friday, discovering on Monday that their integration is dead, and learning the notes mentioned it in paragraph nine. That story gets told, and it attaches to your product's name, not to the release.

There's also a fairness point. The users hit by breaking changes are usually your most invested ones — API integrators, plugin authors, the shop with the old printer. They built on your platform in good faith. Leading with what they must do is the minimum courtesy for breaking their setup.

A compromise that usually satisfies everyone: keep the breaking section short and mechanical (what breaks, who it affects, what to do, in three lines), then give the features the full celebratory treatment immediately after. Total cost to the marketing goal: about ten seconds of reading. Total benefit: nobody's Monday gets ruined by your release notes.

What's actually the difference between an incident report and a runbook? Our team writes great post-incident notes and then nobody can find anything in them during the next incident.

They're written for opposite moments. An incident report is read **afterwards, by people who weren't there, to understand what happened**. A runbook is read **during, by someone tired and under pressure, to decide what to do next**. Almost every difference follows from that.

An incident report is a narrative in past tense: timeline, what we saw, what we tried, what worked, what we'll change. Its value is completeness — the false starts and dead ends belong in it, because they're evidence about the system.

A runbook is a procedure in imperative mood: 'check the pool saturation; if it's at the limit, raise it to 80.' Its value is *selection* — only the steps that worked, in the order to try them, with the decision points made explicit ('if the gateway itself is down, stop and escalate'). The dead ends mostly don't belong, except the expensive ones, which earn a warning line: 'do not purge the queue; we did this once and re-sent 300 messages by hand.'

Your team's problem is the common one: the report is being asked to do the runbook's job. During an incident, nobody can mine a three-page narrative for the next action. The fix is a deliberate second step after each incident — thirty minutes, while it's fresh — that asks three questions of the report:

1. Which steps actually moved us toward resolution? (Those become runbook steps.)
2. Which checks told us which kind of incident this was? (Those become the triage section at the top.)
3. What did we do exactly once, or try and abandon? (Those get flagged or left out — a runbook step should normally be something that has worked more than once, or be labelled as unverified.)

Keep both documents, linked: the runbook cites the incident reports it was mined from, so anyone can trace a step back to its evidence. The report stays the record; the runbook becomes the tool. Teams that merge them end up with a document that's too long to use at 3am and too terse to learn from afterwards.

When I'm building a runbook from incident notes, what do I do with a step that only appears in one incident? Half my team says if it worked once it goes in, the other half says one data point is an anecdote.

Both halves are half right, because 'a step that appears once' is actually three different things wearing one coat:

1. **A step that was only *needed* once.** The incident had a feature the others didn't — a poison message at the head of the queue, say — and the step (dead-letter it) was the correct, validated response to that feature. It goes in the runbook, attached to its condition: 'if the queue is stuck on one message, dead-letter it.' Frequency across incidents is the wrong measure; frequency *given the condition* is the right one, and there it may be 1 of 1.

2. **A step that was done once and worked, but might have been coincidence.** The incident also resolved around the same time for other reasons — someone restarted a service while a deploy was finishing anyway. This one goes in *labelled*: 'done in the Dec 3 incident; unverified.' A label costs nothing and converts an anecdote into a hypothesis the next incident can confirm or kill.

3. **A step that was done once and caused harm.** Purging a queue, failing over 'just to see', widening permissions to get access. This goes in as a prohibition, not a step: 'do not purge the queue — done once, 300 messages re-sent by hand.' Negative knowledge is some of the most valuable content in a runbook precisely because it was expensive to learn.

So the rule isn't include-or-exclude; it's *classify and label*. What you must not do is the silent middle: copying every action from every incident into an undifferentiated checklist. That produces runbooks where the proven core (the steps that appear in every incident) carries the same authority as a one-off improvisation, and at 3am nobody can tell them apart.

A practical format that keeps the peace: print the incident count next to each step — [3 of 3], [1 of 3 — unverified]. Your first half gets their step included; your second half gets its evidential status in plain sight. After the next incident, recount. Steps earn or lose their labels with use, which is exactly how a runbook should age.

We wrote a bunch of runbooks last year and they've quietly rotted — steps referencing tools we retired, thresholds nobody believes. How do we keep them alive without turning it into a bureaucracy?

Runbooks rot for a structural reason: they're written once, by the person who just survived the incident, and then owned by nobody. The fix isn't a review process — it's attaching the runbook's upkeep to events that already happen.

**Three habits that do most of the work:**

1. **The incident closes the loop.** Every incident that *used* a runbook ends with a two-minute question: did every step still work as written? The person who ran it edits it on the spot — a threshold that was wrong, a tool that's been renamed. Editing while the memory is fresh costs minutes; a quarterly audit costs days and finds less, because nobody remembers which step lied.

2. **Every incident that *didn't* use one asks why.** Either there was no runbook (write one from the notes, while they're fresh), or there was and the responder didn't trust it — which is the rot alarm. A runbook the on-call routes around is worse than none, because it still looks authoritative to everyone else.

3. **Date and provenance on the document itself.** Each runbook carries 'mined from incidents of Dec 1, Dec 7, Dec 14; last verified in use on [date]'. That one line tells a 3am reader how much to trust it, and tells you at a glance which runbooks haven't been exercised in a year. Unexercised isn't the same as wrong — but it's the right review queue, in priority order, without a separate audit programme.

**What to skip:** scheduled line-by-line reviews of every runbook, sign-off chains, and format standardisation drives. They feel like rigour and mostly produce documents that are beautifully formatted and quietly wrong, because the reviewers are checking prose, not truth. A runbook's truth can only be tested against incidents.

One more thing: let runbooks shrink. When a step's system is retired, delete the step the week the retirement ships — the retirement ticket is the trigger, not a future cleanup. A shorter runbook that's entirely true beats a comprehensive one with fossils in it, every time, at any hour of the night.

Our FAQ writing keeps getting us in trouble — an agent once wrote that refunds are 'usually approved within a week' and customers have quoted it back at us for months. How do I stop FAQ answers from outrunning what we actually know?

That sentence is the classic FAQ failure: it sounds helpful, it's probably even true most of the time, and it became a promise the moment it was published under your name. Customers quoting it back are behaving entirely reasonably — you wrote it down.

The discipline that prevents it has three rules:

**1. Every answer cites its source — to itself, during drafting.** Write FAQ answers only from documents you're allowed to treat as policy: the help doc, the terms, the price sheet, the manual. If the answer isn't in a source, it isn't in the FAQ. 'What does the source say?' is a much better drafting question than 'what do I know?' — you know all kinds of things that aren't commitments.

**2. Never soften a hard source into a warm one.** Your agent's error was a translation error: the policy presumably said something like 'refunds are decided case by case', and it came out as 'usually approved within a week'. Watch for the three classic softeners — adding a timescale nobody committed to ('within a week'), adding a likelihood ('usually', 'normally'), and adding a reason ('because we value you') that implies an obligation. Quote the policy's actual shape, even when it's less comforting.

**3. Route the unanswerable visibly.** Every FAQ draft should end with a flagged list: questions customers ask that no source covers. That list is a work order for whoever owns the policy — and until they rule, the question gets a human support reply, not a published answer. The flagged list is what stops the next agent from improvising under deadline pressure, because the improvisation is what they're doing when the FAQ has a hole and a customer is waiting.

One operational tip: keep the source next to each published answer in your internal copy (not the public one). When the policy changes, you can find every answer it touches. Most FAQ rot is just policy that moved while the answers stood still.

I'm mining support threads for our FAQ and one angry customer wrote nine messages about a delivery problem. By message count it's our 'biggest issue'. My gut says that's wrong — how should I actually count what customers are asking about?

Your gut is right, and the fix is to change the unit you count. **Count threads (one customer, one issue), not messages.** Nine messages from one person is one data point about what customers ask — and nine data points about how that one interaction went.

Here's why the distinction matters for a FAQ specifically. A FAQ exists to answer the questions the *most customers* will have, before they have to ask. Frequency across customers is the signal. Message volume measures something else entirely: how unresolved an issue felt, how the conversation was handled, how persistent the person is. One furious thread with nine messages usually means one question that got answered badly nine times — which might make it a support-training issue, but it doesn't make the question common.

Practical method:

1. **Reduce each thread to its underlying question**, in the customer's terms: 'how do I pause?', 'why did my bank disconnect?', 'can I get a refund?' Threads that ask two things count once under each.
2. **Tally threads per question.** That's your frequency table, and it's the order your FAQ should be written in.
3. **Then look at the long threads separately.** Sort by message count and read the top few — not for the FAQ, but because a question that takes nine messages to resolve is often a *badly answered* common question. If 'how do I pause?' appears in 4 threads but one of them ran to 12 messages, the FAQ answer probably exists and isn't findable, or the product flow contradicts it.

Two more counting traps. Near-duplicates: 'export my data', 'download my passwords' and 'moving to a new laptop' may be one question (export) wearing three outfits — group by intent or you'll undercount your most common need. And recency: a question that appeared 6 times since a product change two weeks ago outranks one that appeared 8 times across last year. Count over a stated window and say which window you used.

Done this way, your delivery thread gets its correct weight: one thread, one question — plus a flag in a different report, the one about conversations that go wrong.

When a FAQ question can't be answered from our sources, I flag it as an 'escalation'. My manager asked what a good escalation entry actually contains, beyond 'we don't know'. Fair question — what should it have?

A good escalation entry is a small work order that lets someone with authority close the gap in one pass, without re-doing your research. Five elements:

1. **The question, in the customer's words** — plus how often it's being asked and over what window ('asked in 3 of the last 30 days of threads'). Frequency is what turns your flag from a nitpick into a priority; a question asked once may wait, one asked weekly is costing support time now.

2. **What you checked.** Name the sources you searched — the help doc, the price sheet, the manual excerpt, the policy page — so the owner knows the gap is real and doesn't bounce it back with 'it's in the docs' when it isn't. This is the element most escalations skip, and its absence is why they stall.

3. **Why it can't be improvised.** State the risk of guessing in one line: a guessed refund policy becomes a customer commitment; a guessed warranty term is a legal exposure; a guessed safety instruction is worse. This tells the owner the flag is discipline, not laziness.

4. **Who can answer it.** Route to the role that owns the underlying decision — billing policy to whoever sets billing policy, warranty terms to product/legal — not just 'the team'. An escalation addressed to everyone is answered by no one.

5. **What happens meanwhile.** The interim handling: 'support answers this individually by email; no published answer until ruled.' That line protects the next agent from improvising under pressure, which is how the gap usually gets 'filled' badly.

Keep the entry short — if it takes longer to read than to rule on, it won't get ruled on. And keep the list of open escalations visible wherever the FAQ is maintained: an escalation that disappears into a ticket queue is functionally the same as answering the question by guessing, just slower.

My team's status reports are full of 'nearly done', 'almost there', 'just the final touches'. Everything sounds 90% complete for weeks. How do I fix the reporting without becoming the status police?

The problem isn't dishonesty — it's that 'nearly done' is doing three jobs at once, and all three are useless to a reader. It reports effort spent ('I've worked hard on this'), it reports optimism ('the rest looks easy'), and it avoids reporting the one thing that matters: what, concretely, remains.

The fix that works without policing anyone: **ban the adjective, require the remainder.** A status update may not say how close something feels; it must name the unfinished pieces. 'Checkout redesign: payments step remaining' is one line, it's checkable next week, and nobody has to argue about whether it's 80% or 90% — the argument that makes people defensive in the first place.

Why 'nearly done' persists, so you can be kind about it:

- **The last piece is genuinely invisible until you reach it.** The payments step of a checkout is where the edge cases live. Your team isn't lying about the first 90%; they're discovering that the final 10% contains half the work. Naming the remainder surfaces this instead of hiding it.
- **Percentages feel safer than lists.** '90% done' can't be contradicted today. 'Payments step remaining' can be checked on Friday. People reach for the unfalsifiable version when they fear the checkable one will be used against them — so the norm only sticks if the remainder list is treated as information, not as a confession.

Two structural helpers. First, define your statuses as verbs about the work, not feelings about it: *shipped* means a user can use it; *in progress* means someone worked on it this week; *blocked* means it needs something specific from someone specific — and the update must name both. Second, in your own reports, model it ruthlessly: report your own nearly-done items as in-progress with the remainder named. Teams copy the honesty they see above them far faster than the honesty demanded of them.

Within a few weeks the phrase usually dies on its own, because 'payments step remaining' is simply more useful to write — it tells next week's you what to pick up.

I read a status report last week that said 'engagement is up, churn is stabilising, and the migration is on track' — and I realised I couldn't verify a single claim in it. What makes a status report verifiable instead of just plausible-sounding?

A claim is verifiable when a sceptical reader can trace it to evidence without asking you anything. Your three examples each fail in an instructive way:

- **'Engagement is up'** — up by how much, over what period, measured how? The verifiable version: 'weekly active users rose from 4,120 to 4,480 between November 2 and November 30, per the analytics dashboard.' Number, baseline, window, source.
- **'Churn is stabilising'** — 'stabilising' is a story about a trend with no data in it. The verifiable version either gives the series ('3.4%, 3.3%, 3.3% over the last three months') or admits the honest state: 'one month of flat churn; too early to call it stable.' Notice the verifiable version is sometimes *less* impressive — that's the point. Precision costs you adjectives and buys you credibility.
- **'The migration is on track'** — on track against what? The verifiable version: '7 of 15 workstreams done; the two blocked items are X (waiting on legal) and Y (waiting on credentials); the cutover date of January 29 still holds because neither block is on the critical path.' Now a reader can disagree productively — they can check the count, question the critical-path claim, chase the blockers.

The underlying discipline is simple to state: **every claim in the report should be traceable to a source the reader could inspect** — a log, a table, a dashboard, a dated entry. When you draft, keep the sources open next to the draft. When you review someone else's report, ask one question per paragraph: 'where would I look to check this?' If the answer is 'you'd have to ask me', the claim is a rumour wearing a report's clothes.

One more marker of the real thing: verifiable reports include the unfavourable numbers at the same precision as the favourable ones. A report that gives signups to the unit and churn as a vibe has told you exactly where its author stopped being careful.

Half the value of a status report is the blocked list, but ours just says 'blocked' with no context and nothing ever gets unblocked. What should a blocked item actually include?

A blocked item is a request for help wearing a status's clothing. If it doesn't tell the reader exactly what would unblock it and who holds that thing, it isn't a request — it's a lament, and it will sit there week after week, which is what you're seeing.

Every blocked item should carry four things:

1. **The blocker, specifically.** Not 'waiting on approval' but 'waiting on legal to confirm the audit-data retention period'. The specific version lets a reader judge whether the block is reasonable — sometimes blocking is the correct, careful thing to do, and the report should make that visible rather than making the team look stuck.

2. **Who can unblock it.** A person or a named team, not a department-shaped fog. 'Warehouse team — endpoint credentials' gives the meeting someone to go and ask. If you can't name who holds the unblock, that *is* the finding, and it should be reported as such: 'blocked, owner of the unblock unknown' is an escalation all by itself.

3. **How long it's been blocked.** Age changes the meaning completely. Blocked for two days is normal friction; blocked for three weeks is a decision nobody is making. Reports that show age force the conversation that reports without it postpone forever.

4. **What it's blocking.** The downstream cost: 'this gates the audit migration, which gates the old database decommission'. A block on the critical path deserves the meeting's first ten minutes; a block on a side task deserves a line. Without the consequence, all blocked items look equal, and equal-looking items get ignored in order of appearance.

And a rule for the meeting itself: a blocked item may appear in at most two consecutive reports unchanged. The third time, the report doesn't list it again — it escalates it, by name, to whoever can move the person who can move the block. That single rule converts the blocked list from a museum of stalled work into the most useful page of the report.

I take meeting notes and afterwards nobody can agree on what was actually decided versus just discussed. Are there reliable signals in how people talk that tell me which is which?

There are, and they're more reliable than most note-takers expect — because groups usually mark their decisions linguistically whether they mean to or not. Listen for these:

**Signals of a real decision**
- **A named decider or a vote.** 'Ruth, you make the call', a show of hands, a chair saying 'then we're agreed'. Decisions have an authority attached; discussion doesn't need one.
- **A commitment of resources.** A date, a budget line, a person assigned. 'Launch is February 1' spends the company's calendar. 'February might work' spends nothing.
- **Closure language.** 'Decided', 'agreed', 'we'll go with', 'final answer' — followed by the group *moving on*. The strongest signal of all is what happens next: decided items stop being discussed. If the same topic resurfaces twenty minutes later as an open question, it was never decided, whatever words were used.
- **Consequences being arranged.** Someone starts asking 'who tells the team?' or 'what do we need by Friday?' — logistics only make sense downstream of a decision.

**Signals of discussion, however warm**
- **Hedged modals:** 'we should probably…', 'it might be worth…', 'someone could…'. These propose; they don't commit. 'We should probably hire another designer' with a reply of 'I'll think about it' is the textbook non-decision.
- **No owner, no date, no resource.** An 'action' with nobody's name on it is a wish the room shared for a moment.
- **Agreement about values rather than actions.** 'We all agree quality matters here' feels like consensus and decides nothing.

The practical habit: when you hear something that sounds decision-shaped, ask one question in the room — 'is that decided, and who owns it?' It takes five seconds, it's not pedantic (chairs are usually grateful), and it converts your notes from a transcript into a record. Afterwards, write the two lists separately — decisions, and discussed-but-not-decided — and circulate both. The second list is where future misunderstandings go to be prevented.

What makes an action item from a meeting actually usable? Mine come out as things like 'look into the website situation' and three weeks later nobody knows what was meant, let alone whether it happened.

'Look into the website situation' fails every test an action item has to pass. A usable action item has four parts, and the discipline is refusing to write it down until you have all of them — or explicitly marking the one that's missing.

1. **A verb that describes a finishable act.** 'Look into', 'review', 'handle' and 'sort out' are not finishable — there's no state of the world where you can point and say 'done'. Finishable verbs: send, draft, book, confirm, publish, decide, order, notify. If the real action is 'investigate and come back with options', the finishable version is 'bring three options with prices to the January meeting' — the deliverable is the options, not the looking.

2. **An owner — one named person.** Not a team, not 'we'. Committees don't do actions; people do. If the owner is genuinely undecided, write 'UNASSIGNED' in the record rather than leaving a blank: a blank gets misread as someone else's job, while UNASSIGNED is visibly a problem to fix.

3. **An object specific enough to recognise.** 'The website situation' becomes 'the hosting renewal quote' or 'the contact form errors'. Three weeks later, the owner should be able to read the item and know instantly whether it's the thing they did.

4. **A due date or trigger — but only if the meeting actually set one.** This is where note-takers most often invent. If the meeting said 'by Friday', write it. If it didn't, write the item without a date and let it be visibly undated; an invented deadline creates a fake failure next week, and a real one nobody agreed to. If your meetings habitually set no dates, that's a chairing problem to raise — not a gap for the notes to paper over.

A quick test before any action leaves the room: could a stranger, reading only this line, tell you in three weeks whether it happened? 'Priya — update the release calendar to block Friday deploys, from January' passes. 'Look into the website situation' never will.

I'm writing up meeting notes and there's one item where I genuinely can't tell if the group decided it or just leaned that way. The chair has gone home. What do I write?

You write exactly that: that you can't tell. The worst possible outcome isn't an unresolved item in the record — it's a false decision in the record, because a false decision gets acted on, quoted, and built upon, and unwinding it costs ten times what a clarification would have.

Concretely, the entry should have three parts:

1. **What was discussed, fairly.** Summarise the proposal and the direction of the discussion, including who leaned which way if that's clear. 'The group discussed moving the training day to Thursdays. Most speakers favoured it; the rota impact wasn't examined.'

2. **The status, stated as unresolved.** Use a label that can't be misread — 'NOT DECIDED — confirmation needed' — and put the item in the discussed-not-decided section of the record, never in the decisions list with a caveat. Caveats get stripped when records are copied; sections survive.

3. **Who confirms, and how it gets decided.** Name the chair (or whoever held the authority in the room) as the confirmer: 'Chair to confirm whether this was decided; if not, it returns to the January agenda.' That turns your uncertainty into a tiny, answerable task for the one person who can resolve it, and gives the item a route back if the answer is no.

Two things not to do. Don't resolve it by asking the loudest participant afterwards — you'll get their preference wearing the meeting's authority. And don't soften the label to something like 'agreed in principle', which is the phrase organisations use to smuggle undecided things into the decided column; 'in principle' agreements have a way of being quoted without their qualifier.

There's a quiet benefit to doing this visibly: when your records reliably separate 'decided' from 'leaned that way', people start trusting the decided list completely — and chairs start making decisions more explicitly, because they can see the cost of ambiguity landing on their own desk as a confirmation task.

I keep catching our READMEs describing features that don't exist — someone writes the docs from the roadmap instead of the code. How do you keep a README honest?

By changing what the README is allowed to cite. A roadmap describes intentions; a README may only describe the artifact in front of the reader — the code as it exists in this version. Three working rules:

**1. Every claim traces to a file.** Commands come from the manifest or the argument parser, not from memory. Config keys come from the config loader, with defaults copied from the code that sets them. Endpoints come from the route definitions. When you draft a README by touring the codebase file by file — entry point, manifest, config, routes — invention has almost no opportunity to creep in, because you're transcribing, not composing.

**2. Absences get documented too, when users will assume them.** The most damaging README lies are omissions: the CSV tool that never says 'no Excel support', the API whose docs don't mention that two routes need a token. If a feature is plausible, adjacent, and asked about — and it isn't there — one explicit line ('Not supported: …') is worth more than a page of accurate feature description, because it kills the assumption at the moment it forms.

**3. The roadmap lives somewhere else, labelled.** There's nothing wrong with documenting plans — in a ROADMAP file, under a heading that says 'planned, not yet available'. The failure mode is the merged document, where 'will support plugins' sits in the same typeface as 'supports CSV export' and readers reasonably treat both as present tense. Version the README with the code it describes; let plans carry their own dates and caveats.

And a maintenance rule that keeps it true over time: a README change rides in the same commit as the behaviour change, reviewed by the same person. The moment docs become a separate, later task, they become a separate, never task — and the gap between code and docs is exactly where phantom features breed.

Our README says 'just pip install it and run python main.py' but the project actually uses Poetry and the entry point is a console script. A new hire lost an hour to this. What's the right way to write install instructions?

Install instructions are the one part of a README that gets executed verbatim by someone with zero context — so they must be transcribed from the project's own manifest, never written from the author's habits. Your new hire didn't make a mistake; the README gave them instructions for a different project than the one in the repo.

The method:

1. **Open the manifest first** — pyproject.toml, package.json, go.mod, Gemfile, whatever the ecosystem uses. It declares the build tool, the dependencies, and usually the entry point. The README's install section is a *translation* of that file into steps, nothing more.
2. **Use the project's own tool.** If the manifest is Poetry's, the instructions are `poetry install` and the run command is the console script declared under the scripts entry — even if plain pip would *probably* also work. 'Probably works' is how environments diverge: the new hire's pip install resolves different versions, and their first bug becomes an environment ghost nobody can reproduce.
3. **Give the run command exactly as declared.** If pyproject declares `csvslice = "csvslice.main:main"`, the README says `csvslice`, not `python -m csvslice` — the module invocation might work today and break at the next refactor, while the declared entry point is a contract the maintainers have to keep.
4. **Test the instructions on a clean environment.** The author of the README already has everything installed, so their test proves nothing. A fresh container or a colleague's untouched machine, following only the README, either reaches a running program or finds the missing step. This takes ten minutes and is the only real verification install instructions can get.

And when the manifest changes — new build tool, new entry point — the README's install section changes in the same commit. Install instructions rot faster than any other documentation because they describe the project's *packaging*, which changes silently while the code looks the same. Treat the manifest as the source of truth and the README as its mirror, and the next new hire loses zero hours.

Found a fun one: our existing user guide says the export limit is 1,000 rows, but the code says 5,000 — the limit was raised two releases ago and nobody told docs. When code and docs disagree, which wins, and what do I do about the loser?

The code wins — always, and it isn't close. The code is what the system *does*; the guide is a claim about the system. When they disagree, users experience the code's version: someone exported 3,000 rows successfully under a guide that says the limit is 1,000, or worse, designed their process around 1,000 rows they never needed to split. The guide wasn't a different opinion, it was simply wrong, the way a map is wrong when the road moved.

But 'the code wins' comes with three duties toward the loser:

1. **Fix the doc from the code, in the same pass that finds the discrepancy.** Read the actual constant or config value (5,000), check whether it's really a hard limit or a default that can be configured — guides should state which — and correct the guide. Don't split the difference, don't write 'approximately', and don't leave a note saying 'limit may vary': the number in the code is knowable, so know it.

2. **Ask why the doc was wrong, because the answer generalises.** A limit raised two releases ago that never reached docs means behaviour changes aren't flowing to documentation. Somewhere there's a release process with no docs step. Fixing the one number leaves the process that will produce the next wrong number. At minimum, search the guide for every other number that came from the same era — limits, timeouts, defaults — and check each against the code. Discrepancies travel in packs.

3. **Consider the users who believed the doc.** Anyone who built a workflow around the 1,000-row limit did unnecessary work, and anyone who *relied* on it (say, a compliance process that assumed exports couldn't exceed 1,000 rows) has a real problem. A correction note in the changelog — 'the export limit was raised to 5,000 in v2.4; the guide incorrectly stated 1,000 until now' — costs one line and is the difference between a typo and a cover-up.

The one exception to 'code wins': when the doc records an *intention* the code fails to meet — a spec, a contract, a regulatory requirement. Then the disagreement is a bug report against the code, not the doc. The way to tell them apart: ask whether the doc or the code is the thing someone outside the team can hold you to. A user guide is held to the code. A contract is the reverse.

I have to write a version-range summary from a pile of per-version changelogs, and I keep finding the good stuff in the wrong places — a feature users wanted was in a release called 'internals', and a 'major' release was mostly plumbing. How do you read changelogs against the grain like that?

By remembering what a changelog entry actually is: a description of the *work*, written by the person who did it, in the vocabulary of the codebase. Your job is to translate each entry into its *effect on a user* — and the two routinely diverge, in both directions.

Three reading habits do most of the work:

**1. Interrogate the boring words.** 'Rewrote', 'migrated', 'consolidated', 'upgraded the X library' — each of these changed *something* the software does. The question is always: what can a user now do, see, or stop suffering that they couldn't before? A rewritten indexing pipeline that means 'search now finds text inside attachments' is a headline feature wearing a hard hat. Conversely, 'corrected a calibration routine' can mean a safety cut-off now works. The duller the wording around a behaviour change, the more carefully you should read it — engineers understate effects they consider obvious.

**2. Distrust the headings in both directions.** A release titled 'major' or 'the big one' may be a versioning formality — a breaking internal change forces a major number even when users see nothing. A release titled 'maintenance' or 'internals' may carry the range's most important fix. Read the entries, not the banners; the summary you write should be organised by effect (features, speed, fixes, safety), which frees you from the original releases' self-image entirely.

**3. Keep a two-column tally as you read: entries, and user-visible effects.** Some releases will score zero in the second column — that's a finding, not an embarrassment, and your summary should say so in one grouped line ('2.1 and 2.5 contained no user-facing changes'). The tally also protects you at the end: your summary's claims can be checked against the count, and nothing in the pile was silently skipped.

The mindset, in one sentence: the changelog is a witness, not an authority — a truthful one, usually, but answering a different question ('what did we do?') from the one your readers are asking ('what's different for me?').

In a version-range summary, what do I do with the releases that had no user-facing changes at all? My instinct is to give every version its own section so the summary looks complete, but some sections would just say 'bug fixes and improvements' — which I know is a lie, there weren't even visible bug fixes.

Your instinct about completeness is right and your instinct about equal sections is wrong — and the phrase you're refusing to write is exactly the one you should keep refusing. 'Bug fixes and improvements' for a release whose changes were a build pipeline move and a telemetry swap isn't a summary; it's a filler line that teaches readers to distrust the sections that *do* contain something.

The honest treatment has three parts:

**Group them, in one place, in one or two lines.** 'Versions 2.1 and 2.5 contained no user-facing changes: dependency updates, a build pipeline move, and internal refactoring.' That single paragraph *is* the completeness you wanted — a reader can account for every version in the range, and nobody is asked to wade through two empty sections to do it. Completeness means every version is *accounted for*, not that every version gets equal furniture.

**Name what the changes actually were, at the category level.** 'No user-facing changes' alone can sound evasive, as if you're hiding something. Adding the real categories — build, dependencies, internal storage, error reporting — proves the negative. You're not asking readers to trust that nothing happened for users; you're showing them the list and letting them reach the same conclusion.

**Keep the tally visible.** If your summary says '30 entries across the range, 20 user-visible', the grouped paragraph for the zero-impact releases is what makes the arithmetic checkable. Without it, a careful reader counts your sections, gets a number that doesn't match, and wonders what you skipped.

There's a strategic point too. Teams pad summaries because they fear 'two of our seven releases did nothing for users' looks bad. It doesn't — it looks like a team that also does maintenance, which every user with a three-year-old product is quietly grateful for. What looks bad is a summary caught inflating, because then every real claim in it gets re-read with suspicion.

Any rules for writing a summary that spans several versions? I keep either merging facts from different versions into soup, or producing something so version-by-version it's unreadable.

The tension you're feeling is real: version-by-version is accurate but unreadable, theme-by-theme is readable but risks blending facts that were never true at the same time. Four rules keep you on the right side of both:

**1. Tag every fact with its version, even in a themed summary.** 'Refunds to the original payment method (4.5)' costs four characters and prevents the classic soup error — a reader on 4.2 concluding the feature exists for them. Group by theme for readability, but let every bullet carry its version like a luggage tag. If a fact can't be tagged to one version, it probably isn't a fact yet; it's your synthesis, and it should be phrased as one ('across the range, search got faster twice') or dropped.

**2. State the range and the sources up front.** 'Summary of 2.0–2.6, from the per-version changelogs' — one line that bounds the claim. A summary that doesn't say what it covers invites readers to assume it covers everything, including the version that shipped yesterday and isn't in it.

**3. Never merge a change and its later reversal into one neutral line.** If 1.2 raised a limit and 1.4 lowered it again, 'the limit was adjusted' is technically true and practically useless — a user who lived through both needs the story, because their data may carry the marks of each state. Sequences are facts too. The same goes for a feature introduced in one version and renamed in the next: give both names with their versions, or users searching the current name will conclude the summary is about a different product.

**4. Keep a tally and reconcile it before you finish.** Count the entries in the sources; count what your summary describes, groups as internal, or flags. The two numbers must meet. This is the rule that catches the buried feature and the quietly dropped fix — the summary's most common failures are omissions, and omissions are invisible without a count to contradict them.

Follow those and the soup problem mostly dissolves: themes give the reader a map, version tags give them the territory, and the tally guarantees you didn't leave part of the territory off the map.

Every handover I've ever received has been... optimistic. Statuses greener than reality, problems minimised, the leaver clearly writing the reference they wish they were getting. How do you write a handover that's actually honest?

By understanding why handovers drift optimistic, and designing against each cause.

**Cause one: the leaver is the author.** The person with the least incentive to document problems is the one writing them up — every red status feels like a confession. The counterweight is sourcing: build the handover from the systems of record (the ticket tracker, the project board, the register) rather than from the leaver's summary of them. A status pulled from the tracker says 'waiting on vendor'; the leaver's prose would have said 'progressing well with the vendor'. Same ticket, different truth. Interview the leaver for the *unwritten* knowledge — that's what only they can give — and take statuses from the machines.

**Cause two: vague status words.** 'In progress' can mean 'nearly done' or 'started in March and untouched since'. Force statuses to be concrete states with evidence: not 'the migration is going well' but '3 of 6 workstreams in progress, 1 blocked on a vendor fix, 2 not started'. Numbers can't be optimistic in the same way adjectives can — a count either matches the tracker or it doesn't.

**Cause three: the questions get answered.** The leaver half-remembers why a workaround exists, and the handover states it as fact. Honest handovers have a questions section and treat it as a feature: 'the root cause of the fs-old disk problem is unknown' is a *more* useful sentence than a plausible invented cause, because the replacement won't waste January trusting a fiction. If a claim in a handover has no source and no witness, it belongs in the questions, not the facts.

And one structural trick that changes the incentives: have the *receiver* draft the questions section before the leaver writes anything. A handover written to answer a successor's actual questions is grounded in a way a leaver's monologue never is — and a leaver who knows their successor will read it on day one, alone, with a problem, writes a noticeably more honest document.

It feels that way, but the alternative is worse: a handover that answers everything has answered some things by invention. The questions section is what intellectual honesty looks like in document form.

Think about what's actually in a leaver's head. Some of it is solid knowledge they can state: 'payroll runs on the 15th and the last day of the month'. Some of it is *practice without a known reason*: 'I rotate those logs by hand every Friday' — where the honest follow-ups (why does the automatic rotation fail? what exactly breaks if you skip a week?) may be things the leaver themselves doesn't know. 'Root cause unknown; ask Pete to walk through the Friday rotation live before he leaves' is a complete handover entry for that item. The incomplete version would be a confident paragraph of procedure with a guessed diagnosis baked in, which the successor would trust precisely because it looks finished.

There's also a deadline logic to it. Questions have an expiry date: the leaver's last day. A handover written early enough for its questions section to be *used* — asked and answered while there's still time — is a working tool. The answers then get added, attributed and dated, and the document ends up more complete than one that pretended to be complete from the start.

So judge a handover not by whether it contains questions, but by whether its facts are sourced and its questions are specific. 'Various things to discuss' is half-done. Two quick things I see in handovers all the time: passwords pasted into the document 'to be helpful', and nobody ever checking whether the handover actually worked. Settle both for me.

Both are the same underlying failure — treating the handover document as the transfer mechanism, when it's only ever the *map* of the transfer.

**Passwords never go in a handover.** Not because of etiquette, but because of what a handover document is: a file that gets emailed, forwarded, stored in shared drives, and read by people who weren't the intended audience, for years. A password in it has escaped every control the moment it's typed — you can't un-send a document, and you can't rotate a secret nobody remembers sharing. The correct entry is a pointer: 'logins are in the team password manager under Community; IT transfers ownership to the incoming manager.' If you find a password in an existing handover, the password is compromised by definition: rotate it, then fix the document.

**And a handover isn't done when it's written — it's done when it's been read back.** The verification is simple and almost never happens: the successor, after a few days in the role, lists the open items and their states *from their own understanding*, and the two lists are compared. Every difference is a defect in the handover — a status that was ambiguous, a deadline that didn't survive the telling, an item that existed in the leaver's head and never reached the page. A cheaper version, if the leaver has already gone: the successor works from the document alone for a week and notes every question the document failed to answer; those notes become the errata, and the next handover in the team gets better. A handover that was never tested against reality is a draft with good intentions — the read-back is what turns it into a transfer.

I often have to write three versions of the same thing — board, team, customers. I get nervous about which facts to leave out of each. Is there a principled way to decide what each audience's version omits?

Yes, and the principle is reassuring: **you may change emphasis, order, vocabulary and depth — you may never change the facts.** Every version is drawn from one fact set, and any figure that appears in two versions must be identical in both. What varies is selection, and selection follows one question per audience: *what will this reader do with this information?*

- **Executives and boards** act on impact, money, and risk. They get totals, trends, consequences, and what needs deciding. They don't get mechanism — not because it's secret, but because it isn't actionable at their level, and burying the decision in mechanism is its own kind of distortion. What you must never omit for this audience: the bad number, the qualifier, the thing that could reverse the story next quarter.
- **The team who did the work** acts on understanding and credit. They get the mechanism, the detail, and their own contributions named. Omitting the caveats for the team is a particular failure — they will repeat your claims in rooms you're not in, so their version must carry the same honesty about what's proven versus what's projected.
- **Customers** act on what it means for them. They get consequences in their terms ('your payment is safe'), actions they need to take, and timelines in clock time rather than incident-speak. They don't get internal figures that describe them as a resource — revenue per user, churn as a label — not because those are secret, but because they're meaningless from where the customer stands. Meaningless is the criterion, not sensitivity.

The test for any omission: **would this reader, on learning the omitted fact later, feel they'd been misled?** Leaving the connection-pool mechanics out of the customer notice passes that test — no customer feels deceived by not knowing. Leaving the outage duration out would fail it instantly. And the zero-orders-lost figure goes in the *executive* version precisely because omitting it would mislead by silence.

One practical safeguard: draft from a single fact sheet, as a separate document, and keep it. When three versions are each written from the sheet — never from each other — the figures can't drift, and six months later, when someone asks why the board version says 3,214 sessions and the customer version says 'around 3,214 sessions', you can show both came from the same line of the same source. Consistency across audiences isn't about giving everyone the same document. It's about every document being reconcilable with every other.

You keep doing this 'documentation report' thing — claims checked, sourced, corrected, cut. Walk me through the method so my team can run it without you.

Gladly — it's a method, not a talent, and it transfers. Five steps:

**1. Fix the sources before you start.** Decide which documents are sources of record for this draft (the product facts page, the spec, the price sheet, the safety manual) and read *only* those as truth. Everything else — old docs, the previous version, someone's memory — is just more draft. Most audit failures are decided here: if the team can't name the source of record, there is nothing to audit against, and the honest output is 'unauditable until a source exists'.

**2. Extract the claims.** Go through the draft sentence by sentence and list every checkable assertion — every number, date, limit, feature, availability, price, and promise. Ignore tone and structure; you're auditing facts, not editing prose. A one-page draft usually yields 7–12 claims. If a sentence contains two facts, it's two claims.

**3. Give each claim a verdict, and only four verdicts exist.** *Sourced*: the source says this, in substance — keep. *Corrected*: the thing exists but the draft has a detail wrong (a figure, a default, a scope) — fix it to the source's version. *Cut*: no source supports it and there's nothing to correct to — it comes out. *Gap*: the source contains something the draft omits that readers need — an addition, flagged separately from the draft's errors. The discipline is that 'probably true' is not a verdict. A claim you believe but can't source is a cut or an escalation, never a pass.

**4. Show the failures, don't just fix them.** The report lists every corrected and cut claim with the draft's wording and the source's wording side by side. Silent fixing feels efficient and is a loss: the pattern of failures is the most valuable output, because drafts that fail in one direction (always inflating, always softening) tell you how the *next* draft will fail too.

**5. Close with the tally.** Sources read, claims checked, and the counts per verdict. The tally is what makes the report checkable itself — a reader can recount, and 'we audited it' becomes a verifiable statement instead of a vibe.

Run it in that order and your team has the whole method. The only hard part is step 3's discipline, and it gets easier the first time someone has to explain to a customer why the guide promised a backup that never existed.

In your documentation reports you use 'cut', 'corrected', and sometimes 'escalated' for claims that fail the audit. What's the actual difference — when does a bad claim get which verdict?

The three verdicts are three different relationships between the claim and the truth, and choosing between them is the judgement at the heart of the audit.

**Corrected** — *the thing exists; the draft has a detail wrong.* A default of 100 that should be 50. A price of 25 cents that should be 19. Offices numbering three that should be two. Correction is possible because a source states the true version, so the fix is a substitution with a citation. The test: you can point at the source and say 'it should say *this*'. Most numeric and scope errors land here, and correcting them is routine editorial work.

**Cut** — *there is nothing to correct to.* The claim describes something no source supports at all: a reset service that doesn't exist, a 4-hour response promise nobody made, a 'first-ever' superlative nobody can verify. You can't fix these by substitution because there's no true version waiting in a source — the claim was invented, so it leaves. The tell-tale sign you're looking at a cut rather than a correction: fixing it would require someone outside the document to make a *decision* (set a policy, measure a setup time, commit to a response window) before a true sentence could be written.

**Escalated** — *the claim is wrong in a way that makes the document the least of the problem.* The draft instructs something the safety manual prohibits. The draft reveals a practice — clearing jams with the guard up — that may be happening on the floor. Here, quietly fixing the sentence would actually be the worst outcome: it would hide evidence of a real-world problem behind a corrected document. Escalation means the audit stops being an edit and becomes a report to whoever owns the underlying risk, and publication waits for them. The test: if the claim were *true as written*, would someone need to act urgently? If yes, escalate — don't edit.

A useful shorthand for the team: correct what's misstated, cut what's invented, escalate what's dangerous. And note the asymmetry of effort — corrections take minutes, cuts take a decision, escalations take a meeting. Audits that give every failure the same treatment either waste meetings on typos or, far worse, handle a safety contradiction as a typo. The verdict *is* the triage.

Last one: when your audits find bad claims, why do you insist on showing me the cuts and corrections in a report instead of just quietly fixing the document and handing me the clean version? It would be faster.

It would be faster — once. Showing the work buys you three things the clean version can't, and each of them compounds.

**First, the pattern is the diagnosis.** A single corrected figure is a typo. Four corrections that all inflate the product — more users, wider availability, a longer warranty, a faster response — are a drafting culture. If I hand you the clean document, you learn the document is now right. If I hand you the report, you learn *how your documents go wrong*, and you can fix the process: draft from the fact sheet, not from the previous version; route superlatives past a sceptic; make the pricing page the only place prices live. The clean document fixes one publication. The report fixes the pipeline that produces publications.

**Second, some failures aren't mine to resolve.** A cut claim is often a decision in disguise: the 4-hour response promise needs an operational commitment before it can be written truthfully, and I can't make that commitment on the business's behalf. If I quietly delete it, the decision never gets made — it just stops being visible, and the next drafter, working from memory, puts it back. The report forces the decision into the open with an owner attached. The same goes double for anything escalated: a quietly corrected safety instruction is a hazard that got tidied instead of investigated.

**Third, the report is the audit's own evidence.** 'We checked it' is a claim, and claims are what got us here. A report that lists sources read, claims checked, and verdicts given can itself be checked — you can recount it, spot-check a correction against the source, disagree with a verdict. A silently fixed document asks for the same blind trust that produced the original errors.

There's a smaller, human reason too. The person who drafted the document learns from seeing their claims' verdicts — specifically, which of their habits (rounding up, softening, assuming) the audit caught. Hand them a clean version and they'll make the same three mistakes in the next draft, because nobody ever showed them the shape of the last three. The report is slower the way teaching is slower than doing — and for the same reason worth it.
